title: Six Months Into the Iran War, the United States Has No Good Options | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Six months into the U.S.-Iran war, Lindsay argues Washington has no good options: military escalation is blocked by a shortage of defensive interceptors, and the new Operation Economic Outcast risks antagonizing China—which buys over 80 percent of Iran's oil and has already forced Trump to retreat on tariffs by threatening critical minerals. Gulf allies are hedging via the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement and the Abraham Accords, and a likely U.S. military drawdown from the region could prove a mixed blessing.

insights.claim: Trump predicted the war with Iran would last four to five weeks and has repeatedly declared victory, but Iran's regime has neither collapsed nor capitulated despite intense U.S. and Israeli air strikes that killed many prewar leaders.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: The gap between declared victory and a persistent stalemate signals the conflict-risk premium is here to stay, not resolving.
insights.quote: President Donald Trump confidently predicted at the war's start that it would last “four to five weeks.”
insights.locator: Six months into the U.S. war with Iran

insights.claim: A rickety ceasefire agreed in April and extended in June continues to hold, but tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains far below prewar levels.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Suppressed Hormuz tanker traffic keeps oil prices elevated even under ceasefire—an ongoing energy-market drag.
insights.locator: A rickety ceasefire agreed to in April

insights.claim: Trump has repeatedly threatened more destructive attacks on Iran only to back down because the U.S. military lacks the defensive interceptors needed to protect U.S. allies and bases in the region.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: An interceptor shortage is the hard constraint capping U.S. escalation—a concrete military-supply limit shaping the war's ceiling.
insights.quote: Trump has periodically threatened to launch even more destructive attacks on Iran, only to back down because the U.S. military lacks the defensive interceptors

themes.theme: Economic Outcast and the China constraint

insights.claim: Trump vowed an 'Economic D-Day' and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled Operation Economic Outcast, which for now leans on threats to punish countries that refuse to tighten the noose on Iran rather than steps to compel them.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: The pivot to economic pressure is rhetoric-heavy and compulsion-light—signaling the U.S. is boxed in on follow-through.
insights.quote: he vowed last week to unleash an “Economic D-Day” that will be “the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country!”

insights.claim: The secondary sanctions Washington is proposing could, in Bessent's own words, 'blow up the global financial system,' which is why the plan leans on threats rather than enforcement.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: The self-acknowledged systemic risk of secondary sanctions caps how far the U.S. can actually go—limiting the tail-risk to markets from full enforcement.
insights.quote: The so-called secondary sanctions that Washington is proposing could, in Bessent's words, “blow up the global financial system.”
insights.locator: There is good reason for that.

insights.claim: China buys more than 80 percent of Iranian oil exports and has already forced the Trump administration to abandon steep tariffs on Chinese goods by threatening to cut U.S. access to critical minerals, with Xi Jinping set to visit the White House next month.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: China's leverage—Iran's main oil buyer plus critical-minerals chokehold—means any real isolation of Iran collides with U.S.-China dependency; watch the Xi visit.
insights.quote: China buys more than 80 percent Iranian oil exports, and it has already forced the Trump administration to abandon steep tariffs on Chinese goods by threatening to cut U.S. access to critical minerals.
insights.locator: There is good reason for that.

insights.claim: The United States has no good options: military escalation risks Iranian strikes on Arab neighbors and U.S. bases, while economic escalation antagonizes China and risks significant retaliation, leaving Washington hoping a naval blockade forces Iran to sue for peace.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: The core thesis—no good options—implies a prolonged, unresolved standoff and persistent regional and oil-price risk.
insights.quote: The United States has no good options to compel Iran to meet its demands.

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Pakistan and Turkey, but its unreleased text and the fact that Pakistan and Turkey did not help when the Houthis fired on Saudi Arabia forty-eight hours after signing cast doubt on claims it offers NATO-like protections.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: The new Gulf alliance may be weaker than billed—hedging optics more than a credible mutual-defense pact.
insights.quote: Pakistan and Turkey certainly did not, as Steven put it, “send the cavalry to help” when the Houthis fired on Saudi Arabia just forty-eight hours after the agreement was signed.
insights.locator: U.S. allies in the region are hedging

insights.claim: The UAE is placing its chips on deepening the Abraham Accords rather than following Riyadh into the Mecca pact, and the real rift between the two regional powers could complicate U.S. diplomacy going forward.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: A genuine Saudi-UAE split fragments Gulf strategy—two divergent security bets complicate U.S. coordination in the region.

insights.claim: The U.S. military presence in the Gulf will likely diminish in the years to come as the Iran war ushers in a new regional order, but a less-involved United States could still face regional events that harm its interests.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: A structural U.S. drawdown is underway—reshaping the Gulf security order and the risk that regional actors ordering the region produce continued conflict.
insights.quote: the “Iranians, the Saudis, the Turks, the Israelis, and others are going to try to order the region [in a way] that best serves their interests. And there's the possibility for continued conflict and chaos as a result.”
insights.locator: The U.S. military presence in the Gulf
